docs.contenu:
🎯 Objectives
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
- Review and use the main English tenses accurately: present, past and perfect forms.
- Understand the difference between simple, continuous and perfect aspects.
- Choose the right tense according to time markers and context.
- Avoid the most common tense mistakes in writing and speaking.

🔍 Warm-up
Look at three sentences about the same action:
- "I write reports." (a habit)
- "I am writing a report." (happening now)
- "I have written the report." (finished, result matters now)
The verb is almost the same, but the TENSE and ASPECT change the meaning completely. This lesson helps you master those choices.

I. PRESENT TENSES
📘 Rules and definitions
- Present simple: facts, habits and general truths. Form: base verb (+ s in the third person). "Water boils at 100 degrees." "She works in Tunis."
- Present continuous: actions happening now or around now, and future arrangements. Form: am/is/are + verb-ing. "They are studying for the exam." "We are meeting the teacher on Monday."
- Present perfect: past actions with a link to the present, or experiences. Form: have/has + past participle. "I have finished my homework." "She has visited Rome twice."

📝 Grammar patterns and usage
Time markers guide your choice:
- Present simple: always, usually, every day, never.
- Present continuous: now, at the moment, currently, these days.
- Present perfect: already, yet, just, ever, never, since, for.
"Since" points to a starting time ("since 2020"); "for" points to a length of time ("for three years").

✏️ Worked examples
- "My brother usually walks to school, but today he is taking the bus." (habit vs. now)
- "We have lived here since 2019." (started in the past, still true)
- "Have you ever eaten Tunisian couscous?" (experience up to now)

II. PAST TENSES
📘 Rules and definitions
- Past simple: finished actions at a definite past time. Form: verb-ed or irregular. "They arrived yesterday." "He wrote the letter last week."
- Past continuous: an action in progress in the past, often interrupted. Form: was/were + verb-ing. "I was reading when the phone rang."
- Past perfect: an action completed BEFORE another past action. Form: had + past participle. "When we arrived, the film had already started."

📝 Grammar patterns and usage
The past perfect shows which action happened first:
- "She had left before he called." (first: she left; second: he called.)
Use the past continuous for the background action and the past simple for the shorter, interrupting action: "While they were talking, the lights went out."

✏️ Worked examples
- "Last summer we travelled to the south and visited Tozeur." (past simple)
- "It was raining when the match began." (past continuous + past simple)
- "By the time help arrived, the fire had spread to the roof." (past perfect)

III. FUTURE AND PERFECT CONTINUOUS FORMS
📘 Rules and definitions
- will + verb: instant decisions, predictions, promises. "I will help you."
- be going to + verb: plans and intentions, or evidence-based predictions. "Look at those clouds; it is going to rain."
- Present perfect continuous: an action that started in the past and is still continuing, focus on duration. Form: have/has been + verb-ing. "She has been studying for two hours."
- Future continuous / perfect can also appear: "This time tomorrow, I will be travelling."

📝 Grammar patterns and usage
Compare the perfect and the perfect continuous:
- "I have painted the fence." (finished, result: it is painted.)
- "I have been painting the fence." (activity, maybe not finished; explains why you are tired.)
Choose "will" for a decision made at the moment of speaking and "going to" for a plan decided earlier.

🛠️ Writing method
To choose a tense, ask three questions:
1. WHEN did/does the action happen: past, present or future?
2. Is it finished, in progress, or repeated?
3. Is there a link to another time (before, since, for)?
Then match your answers to the correct tense form.

👀 Notes
Some verbs (know, like, want, believe, understand, belong) are "state" verbs and are not normally used in continuous forms. Say "I understand", not "I am understanding". This rule catches many learners in exams.

⚠️ Common mistakes
- Using the present simple for an action happening now: WRONG "I read now"; RIGHT "I am reading now".
- Mixing "since" and "for": "since three years" is wrong; use "for three years".
- Forgetting the past participle after "have": WRONG "I have went"; RIGHT "I have gone".
- Using "will" for a fixed plan instead of "going to".
- Putting state verbs in the continuous: "I am wanting".

⭐ To remember
- Simple = complete or habitual; continuous = in progress; perfect = linked to another time.
- Present perfect uses have/has + past participle; past perfect uses had + past participle.
- "since" + point in time, "for" + length of time.
- State verbs avoid the -ing form.

🔗 Applications
Accurate tenses make your argumentative and for-and-against essays clear and mature. They also help you narrate events, report facts, and speak confidently in the Baccalauréat oral and written papers.

enonce.question:
Complete the following sentences with the correct form of the verbs in brackets using the present perfect simple or continuous. 
1. She ______ (study) English for three years now. 
2. They ______ (not/see) each other since last summer. 
3. How long ______ you ______ (know) your best friend? 
4. He ______ (work) on this project since January.
Put the verb in the correct present tense: 'Water ______ (boil) at 100 degrees Celsius.'
Choose 'since' or 'for': 'They have lived in Sfax ______ five years.'
Put the verb in the past simple: 'Yesterday, she ______ (write) a long email.'

Rewrite the following sentences using the correct form of the verbs in brackets with the past perfect simple or continuous. 
1. By the time we arrived, the film ______ (already/start). 
2. She was tired because she ______ (clean) the house all morning. 
3. They ______ (live) in this city for five years before they moved. 
4. He ______ (wait) for two hours when the bus finally arrived.
Complete with the correct tense (past simple or past continuous): 'I ______ (read) a book when the lights ______ (go) out.'
Choose present perfect or past simple: 'She ______ (visit) Rome twice, but she ______ (not go) there last year.'
Correct the mistake: 'I am wanting a cup of tea right now.'
Use the past perfect: 'When we arrived at the cinema, the film ______ (already/start).'
Choose 'will' or 'be going to': 'Look at those dark clouds! It ______ rain.'
Present perfect or present perfect continuous? 'She is tired because she ______ (study) all afternoon.'

Choose the correct option (A, B, or C) to complete each sentence with the appropriate tense (future perfect simple or continuous).
1. By next year, she ______ (teach) for ten years.
   A. will have taught
   B. will have been teaching
   C. will teach
2. They ______ (finish) the project by the time you get here.
   A. will finish
   B. will have finished
   C. will be finishing
3. By the end of this month, he ______ (work) in this company for twenty years.
   A. will work
   B. will have worked
   C. will have been working
4. When you come back, we ______ (decorate) the house for three hours.
   A. will decorate
   B. will have decorated
   C. will have been decorating

Rewrite this paragraph, putting every verb in brackets into the correct tense: 'Last weekend, we (decide) to visit the old medina. While we (walk) through the narrow streets, we (meet) an old friend who (live) there since childhood. We (never see) such a lively market before.'

Find and correct the FOUR tense mistakes: 'I have went to the library yesterday. I am knowing the librarian for years. While I read, my phone was ringing. I have finished my project since three days.'
Write a short paragraph (4-6 sentences) about your day so far. Use at least the present perfect, the past simple and the present continuous, and underline one example of each.
